chapters.title: The Boy Who Was Given Away

blocks.text: Lawrence Joseph Ellison was born on ==17 August 1944== in New York City. His mother, Florence Spellman, was 19 and unmarried. His father was an Italian-American military pilot who was not part of the picture. Ellison would grow up knowing nothing about him.

Florence tried to raise the baby alone, and for nine months she managed. Then he caught pneumonia and nearly died. She could not hold a job and nurse a sick child at the same time. So she sent him to her aunt and uncle in Chicago, Lillian and Louis Ellison, who adopted him and gave him their surname.
Nine months old. The richest-man story begins with a sick baby on a journey.

blocks.text: The man named after an immigration station

Louis Ellison was the biggest force in the house. He left Russia in 1905 as a Jew fleeing persecution. As the family told it, he was hidden in a hay cart to get out of Crimea, then put on a steamer across the Black Sea. He carried two things: a gold locket and a brass samovar for boiling tea.

He reached New York, dropped a Russian name Americans struggled with, and took a new one from the place he had just landed: Ellis Island. So the surname on the world's most famous database fortune is really a port of entry. Louis later moved to Chicago, married, had two children, and built up property in real estate.

Then the Great Depression wiped the business out. By the time Larry arrived, Louis was a modest public-housing auditor. Larry's mother Lillian, Louis's second wife, kept the books at a local dairy. The three of them lived in a two-bedroom apartment. __This was not a poor home and not a rich one. It was a home haunted by money that used to be there.__

For example: Larry later described Louis as a millionaire, a champion tennis player and a candidate for Congress who lost his money, his wife and the election in a single year. His biographer Mike Wilson went looking. He checked Chicago newspapers, the Illinois State Archives and the Chicago Historical Society, and found no trace of a campaign or a famous fortune. Adda Quinn, Larry's first wife, remembered Louis as a very quiet accountant.
Read that twice. Some legends are easier to tell than to prove.

photo.caption: The old South Shore Country Club in Chicago, now a cultural centre, seen in 2008. It stood in the lakeside neighbourhood where Larry spent his teens.
photo.author: Zol87 from Chicago, IL, USA

blocks.text: Lunch at somebody else's table

Wilson places the family on Chicago's North Side for Larry's early years. Larry went to Eugene Field school nearby. Most mothers in the area were home at midday to feed their kids. Lillian was at work, so she arranged for another family to give him lunch.

Small detail, big picture. He was an only child in the house, because Louis's two children from the first marriage were already grown. He had a warm mother who worked, and a stern father who was much older. In a 1997 interview he named her as the one who backed him when he asked who had been supportive.
I don't think my personality has changed much since I was five years old.
blocks.who: Larry Ellison, Academy of Achievement interview, 1997

blocks.text: What was that five-year-old like? By his own account, he was the kid who kept asking why. He remembered teachers who said something he thought was untrue, and who only wanted it repeated back. He called the habit of doubting experts the most important part of his personality. He also admitted it was painful for everyone around him, at home and in class.

He was good at maths and science, and he had a theory for why he liked them: people enjoy what they are good at. He also enjoyed chess, and at some stage played it in tournaments. Puzzles with clear rules suited him. A puzzle never told him he was wrong just because it was older than him.
Notice the pattern: he loved anything where logic beats rank.
The day the family story cracked

At ==12==, he found out he was adopted. Nobody had told him before. Even then, he was not told the full truth. He did not learn until he was an adult that the woman raising him was a blood relative, his birth mother's own aunt. So the mother he adored was really his great-aunt.

How much did it matter? He has given two answers. In 1997 he said he did not put much of his personality down to the adoption, and that his father mattered far more. But he also told Wilson it was a tender subject, and that it is hard for a child to wonder whether he belongs in his own family. He once told a friend that trying hard to succeed was partly how he coped.

For example: it took him until 1991, in his forties and already very rich, to look for Florence. He hired a private investigator, who found her within two months. Vanity Fair reported that he stared at the phone number for two weeks before dialling. The first call lasted about five minutes, because, he said, everyone needed a break.
Two weeks staring at a phone number. Billions don't fix everything.
Was it really a tough neighbourhood?

Here is a question worth asking of any founder's origin story. Ellison has often said he grew up in a bad area on the South Side, and told the Smithsonian he did not know it was bad until he left. Press articles then called it rough, and one said he grew up poor in a tenement.

Wilson dug in and disagreed. In his telling, the family was not poor and the area was stable and middle class when Larry lived there, with lawyers, professors and shop owners as neighbours. Louis's grown daughter Doris used to joke that every new article made the old neighbourhood sound worse. Ellison's own words have shifted too: in one interview they had no money but were not poor, in another they had no idea they were poor.
When a legend sounds too perfect, check the archives. Always.

blocks.title: Use the doubt, do not copy it
blocks.text: Someone close to you may decide you will not make it. You cannot always change their mind. You can decide what that doubt becomes: a wound you carry, or a fuel you burn. But be honest about your own story while you do it. A true hard start is enough.

At ==13==, Larry refused to have a bar mitzvah. For a Jewish boy in a family that went to synagogue regularly, this was a loud thing to do. He had tried to study the Torah to please his parents, but he said his mind drifted within seconds. He did not believe the stories were literally true, and he would not stand up and pretend.
Thirteen, and already refusing to fake it. Look at the nerve.

Around 1959, when he was about 15, the family moved across town to South Shore. He had started at Sullivan High School and now switched to South Shore High. Home was an upstairs flat with two bedrooms and one bathroom, in a building of four flats. Next door lived Doris, Louis's grown daughter, and her husband David Linn.

That new neighbourhood had its own hard edges. In the 1920s, wealthy Protestant families held parties at the lakefront country club. Jewish families who moved in later were kept out of it, so they built their own social world. It was a place that cared about education, and most South Shore High students went on to college.
Invisible in class, loud everywhere else

You might expect a future tech giant to be the star of his school. He was not. He joined no official clubs and played no varsity sport. South Shore High had an honours programme, and he was not in it. The class valedictorian later remembered him as quiet, withdrawn and outside the main crowd.

__The trouble was not brains. He read what he chose to read, not what he was told to read.__ He said later that refusing conventional wisdom got him into a lot of trouble in a school system built on conformity, and served him very well in life. Yet his friend Rick Rosenfield remembered a different boy: intense, opinionated and loud, with an answer for everything.

For example: Rosenfield told Vanity Fair he never saw real academic interest in Larry, but had no doubt he would do something extreme with his life. Rosenfield did all right too. He went on to co-found the California Pizza Kitchen restaurant chain.
Your school friends may build things too. Keep them close.

One of the few groups he did join was a Jewish high-school fraternity, Tau Omicron Mu, whose members called themselves the Tommies. They threw dances and competed against other fraternities at basketball, football and softball. Every year the South Side fraternities also marched and sang rewritten pop songs at a hotel ballroom show. Most families came to watch. Larry's apparently never did.
What he got up to

He had the kind of pull that made other teenagers follow him into bad ideas. His friend Dennis Coleman recalled trips to the local laundromat, where the boys climbed inside the big dryers and rode them, door open so they would not suffocate. The friends had a word for this: laundernating. Once they came across a house under construction and tried to push down a wall with their bare hands. They very nearly did.

For example, a few more real details from his friends. While other boys got haircuts at home from their fathers, Larry paid a professional barber on 71st Street known as Baltimore George. While others played rock music, he preferred show tunes. And for a while he answered the home phone as if he were an official at the Russian embassy.

Basketball was his great love. He would not play for the school team, because that meant obeying a coach. Instead he spent hours shooting at the YMCA, calling himself the Kid and giving a running commentary on his own moves. He also broke his nose several times on the court, which is a very Larry way to spend a teenage afternoon.
No coach allowed. That habit never really left him.
The war at home

The fights with Louis never stopped. Louis loved America with an immigrant's gratitude and believed the government, the police and teachers were basically always right. Larry thought that was absurd and said so. Louis told him he would have to fall in line eventually. Coleman remembered tension and angry words whenever he visited the small apartment.

Then came the line that would follow Larry for life. Louis kept telling him, over and over, that he would amount to nothing. Once, in a game, Larry got mixed up and scored a basket for the other team, and a newspaper mentioned it. According to Larry, Louis kept the clipping so he could bring it out and embarrass him.

Years later Ellison offered a dry thank-you. He told Wilson that fire either destroys you or tempers you, that his father had been powerful motivation, and that he would not recommend the method to any parent. As he got older he simply stopped arguing, since he could not win Louis over and the arguments only upset him.
Told you would fail? Join the club. Now prove them wrong.
The two grown-ups he did admire

He found his role models next door and down the road. Dennis Coleman's father, Harold, was an industrial chemist and college professor with a University of Chicago doctorate. Larry peppered him with questions on everything from relativity to pilots' pay, and he alone among the boys called him Dr. Coleman. What he loved was the method: gather evidence, reason from it, and stop there.

For example: Dennis Coleman remembered Larry turning up with a bag of new clothes from the Marshall Field department store. He had returned his worn-out sweaters and shirts, claimed they were faulty, and walked out with fresh ones. Dennis found it hilarious. His father was appalled and told Larry it was dishonest. Asked decades later, Ellison said it could have happened, but he did not remember it.

The other hero was his brother-in-law, David Linn, who studied law at the University of Chicago, taught at Northwestern and later became a judge. Ellison called him the most visibly successful adult in his life. He would later name his first child David after him. Linn worked constantly, though, so Larry saw less of him than he wished.
First money, first car, first stories

Teenage Larry was embarrassed by the family car, a two-tone 1956 Dodge with push-button gears and no real speed. He rarely invited friends home. So he worked summers as a ==lifeguard== and saved up until he could buy a Sunbeam Alpine, a small convertible sports car. It is the first money-making we can document in his life, and he spent it on how he looked to the world.

He had also found a cheaper way to improve his life: he improved the story. Wilson describes a teenager who was a gifted storyteller, adding funny, flattering, hard-to-disprove details when the facts felt too dull. Rosenfield believed Larry truly believed it all. Coleman thought Larry knew exactly what he was doing, and still said you always had a good time with him.
Selling a future that isn't real yet. Founder superpower, founder danger.

Everyone expected one thing of him. On the South Side, medicine was seen as the top of all professions, and his family, teachers and girlfriend all wanted him to be a doctor. He dreamed of USC medical school and a life in Los Angeles. At 17, he graduated from South Shore High in 1962 with that plan in his head and no real love for the subject.

blocks.title: Being ignored at school proves nothing
blocks.text: No honours programme, no clubs, no team. If you judged him at 16, you would have missed him entirely. Grades measure one kind of obedience. What he had instead was curiosity, nerve and a hunger to be seen. Those can build a life, but they need honest direction.

In September 1962 he rode onto the University of Illinois campus at Urbana-Champaign on a three-wheeled Harley bought cheap at a police auction. He was pre-med. He did well in what he liked and ignored what he did not. Later he called his comparative anatomy class a pointless kind of torture, especially the dissection labs.

photo.caption: Altgeld Hall at the University of Illinois, seen in 2010. Larry spent two years on this campus and left without a degree.
photo.author: Kevin Dooley on Flickr

blocks.text: Finals week, May 1964

At the end of his second year, Lillian was dying of kidney cancer at Billings Hospital in Chicago. He knew she was ill. He says he did not let himself see that she was dying, even though she was in a cancer hospital. She died at the start of finals week. His family said she would have wanted him to sit his exams. He walked out instead and never returned.

He was 19. He told Vanity Fair she had been his only support system growing up. And here is the detail that stops you: __he did not tell his closest friends.__ Years later, when Wilson asked them, they remembered nothing about it. Rosenfield did not even know why his friend had left college.
Nineteen, grieving alone, and telling nobody. Remember this when he seems arrogant later.

So did he flunk or did he leave? Both claims exist. Vanity Fair and the Academy of Achievement say he won a science student of the year award. BusinessWeek reported in 1995 that records showed he was dismissed for not keeping a C average, after skipping finals two semesters in a row. His own explanation is the one you just read. The university would not tell Wilson its reason.

That summer he drove to Northern California for the first time, and stayed with his friend Chuck Weiss. He had seen the early hippie scene on television and wanted to look. Back in Chicago, he could not stop talking about how free it felt. He also spent another summer on lifeguard duty.
The accidental skill

In autumn 1964, aged 20, he enrolled at the University of Chicago. He found it far more stimulating. A physics class required students to program an ==IBM 1401== computer, and that small requirement changed everything. Nobody planned it. He was still telling people he would be a doctor.

He finished his programs faster than anyone else, so the university offered him a job. Very quickly he worked out that being paid per program beat being paid per hour. Then he took consulting work for local businesses. By his own account he was soon out-earning a tenured professor, which felt pretty cool. __He had stumbled onto a skill that paid far better than lifeguarding.__
Very important for students: charge for results, not for hours.

For example: why did he love it? He explained it through sport. Freud said maturity is the ability to wait for your reward, but a programmer gets a result in hours. It is like a basketball shot, where you know within seconds whether you won or lost. Computers also knew nothing about fashion. They just followed logic.

photo.caption: The University of Chicago's main quadrangles, seen in 2015. Records show Larry was registered here for just one semester.
photo.author: Ndshankar

blocks.text: The university's records show he was registered for only one semester. He actually spent much of that time around Northwestern University in Evanston with Dennis Coleman and a new friend, Steve Abramowitz. They recalled some of the happiest days of their lives, and never thought to ask how he was passing classes he rarely attended.

For example: one night, Coleman recalled, police stopped Larry's Sunbeam for speeding along Chicago's Outer Drive with friends squeezed in the back. Larry instantly said he was a medical resident rushing to observe a brain operation at Michael Reese Hospital. The officer was so convinced that he offered an escort. Larry politely declined it and got no ticket.
Terrible behaviour. Also, that is what a future salesman looks like at 20.

The doctor story was also collapsing in private. Coleman remembered being shown an acceptance letter from USC's medical school that looked off to him, though Ellison says Coleman is mistaken and that he only applied. He then drove to Michigan to propose to his long-time girlfriend. She told him she had been seeing someone else for nine months. Around that time he gave up on medicine.

And the college story lived on for decades. A former Oracle executive told Wilson he had heard Larry claim an advanced physics degree from Chicago. In 1988 The New York Times printed that he held bachelor's and master's degrees in physics from there. Ellison later said he regretted not correcting such errors, but denied ever lying about his credentials.
Don't. Dropping out is fine. Pretending you didn't always comes back.
Berkeley, 1966: one car, no plan

With Lillian gone, home got worse. He told Vanity Fair that Louis had started drinking and that it was no fun there. In summer 1966, aged 21, he packed jeans, T-shirts, a leather jacket and a guitar. All his money had gone on a turquoise 1964 Thunderbird convertible, because arriving in style mattered. Louis said he would never make it alone.

He reached Berkeley with just enough cash for fast food and a few tanks of petrol. He walked into an employment agency looking for programming work, and they offered him a job at the agency itself. Working there was Adda Quinn, a student who found him the most fascinating man she had ever met. They married on 23 January 1967, and no one from his family came.

He told Adda he had finished college and was in graduate school, Wilson reports. In truth, Berkeley's records showed him enrolled only in summer 1966, and after that he seems to have just sat in on classes. Money stayed tight. He later claimed to have lived on dime packets of Kraft macaroni and cheese.
Dime macaroni and a flashy Thunderbird. Priorities, at 22.
The weekend programmer

For the next eight years he drifted from job to job: Wellsco Data Systems, Fireman's Fund insurance, Wells Fargo Bank. The work meant minding big IBM mainframes, hanging tapes, backing up data and keeping things running. He chose night and weekend shifts on purpose, because few people wanted them. The couple put tinfoil on the windows so he could sleep during the day.

The weekdays were for freedom. In the book Softwar, he says programming let him fool around through his twenties. Monday to Friday he would be climbing in Yosemite, kayaking rivers or cycling down the California coast. He has also said he worked there as a river guide and rock-climbing instructor. __He was earning just enough to buy back his own time.__

photo.caption: Yosemite Valley from Tunnel View, seen in 2013. Ellison said the valley was one of only two things that ever left him stunned.
photo.author: Diliff

blocks.text: For example: he and his college friend Chuck Weiss used to sit on San Francisco's Telegraph Hill, picking out apartment buildings they would buy one day. They daydreamed about a giant company, and Larry even named it: ==Universal Titanic Octopus==. Weiss later worked at Oracle. He told Vanity Fair that sometimes dreams come true.
A broke guy on a hill, naming his empire. Start there.

In 1970 he and Adda put down a deposit on a $30,000 house in Oakland. He threw himself into fixing it up. Adda once watched him rip an expensive strip of wallpaper off the wall and crush it, because the pattern was a tiny bit crooked. Louis, now old, came to live with them for a while. The two men never found peace.

Money was the running fight. Together they earned about $1,600 a month. He still bought a thousand-dollar bicycle. Then he took a sailing class at Berkeley Marina, fell in love with the water, and borrowed $3,000 for a 34-foot boat while still paying off a smaller one. By his own admission the money stress fell on Adda, not him.

items.label: of bouncing between jobs after Berkeley

blocks.text: The promise in the therapist's office

In 1974 Adda decided to leave. She agreed to one session with a therapist to help him through it. There, she says, he suddenly promised that if she stayed he would become a millionaire and she could have anything she wanted. He had never spoken this way before. She told him to go ahead and do it for himself. She took nothing and walked away.

Ellison remembers the session and calls the counsellor an idiot, but he does recall saying something like that. He says everyone around him seemed sure success would never come his way. In his USC speech he tells it differently: she called him unambitious, she called the sailboat idea stupid, and she kicked him out. Either way, __this was the moment he stopped trying to be what others wanted.__

He bought the boat and lived aboard at Berkeley Marina with his cat. His family was still angry about medical school, his marriage was over, and for the first time, he said, he was not disappointed in himself. He felt sure he could survive in the world, and a huge fear lifted. He was around 30, with no degree and no company.

photo.caption: Berkeley Marina today. Ellison took his sailing class here and later lived on a boat here with his cat.
photo.author: Tbo47

blocks.text: Thirty and divorced, living on a boat. It is not too late.
Silicon Valley, finally

Slowly he worked out that the most interesting programming jobs sat in a cluster of companies south of Stanford. In 1973 he joined Amdahl in Sunnyvale, a startup trying to take IBM's customers with a faster, compatible mainframe, the 470 V/6. He knew IBM machines, so his job was teaching Amdahl's engineers. A colleague named Stuart Feigin remembered him above all for talking non-stop, about himself, about everything, and about how rich he would be.

Amdahl also opened a door to Japan. Fujitsu owned a large stake, so a work trip took him to Kyoto. Its gardens stunned him the way Yosemite had, and he fell in love with Japanese design. He later drew another lesson from Gene Amdahl's story: avoid venture capital, which he said cost Amdahl his job. Then the company ran short of cash and laid Larry off.

For example: a couple of years later Ellison phoned Feigin, said he was starting a company and promised to make him rich. Feigin earned $35,000 a year at Amdahl and told himself Larry was a flake with no chance. Larry could not even turn up to lunch on time. Feigin joined later with less stock, and estimated that the delay cost him a couple of billion dollars.
Very expensive lunch. Judge the idea, not only the punctuality.
The two men who mattered most

Next came Ampex in Sunnyvale, an audio and video equipment company. He disliked the manager assigned to him and simply refused to work for him. He chose Bob Miner, a quiet, gifted programmer born in Cicero, Illinois, to immigrant parents from what is now northern Iran. Then one day he mentioned his ex-wife's name in Miner's office. A passing colleague stuck his head in: Adda had been his high-school biology lab partner.

That colleague was Ed Oates, on only his second day at the company. One of Silicon Valley's great partnerships began with a chance remark about a frog-dissection partner. Together they worked on a CIA-funded plan to store a trillion bits of data on videotape, searching at a thousand inches per second. The CIA's code name for the project was ==Oracle==.

photo.caption: An Ampex 601 tape recorder, photographed in 2016. Ampex was best known for audio and video recording equipment like this.
photo.author: Sverma

blocks.text: They played chess, ate long lunches and left for tennis around three. Oates recalled that Miner wrote code between matches while Larry talked about getting rich and famous. Ellison insists he was a very good programmer. Long-time Oracle engineer Ken Jacobs later repeated the company legend that the founders rated Larry their worst coder and sent him out to sell, though Jacobs doubted that was fair. At lunch the three complained about bosses, pay and seniority, and joked that they did 140 percent of the work. When the videotape system failed, they blamed management, and started to wonder what they would do differently.
Very important: complaining about your bosses can be market research. Take notes.
The bid that started everything

By 1976 Ellison had moved to Precision Instrument, which later became Omex. He was now a vice-president, the first time he had been in charge of anything. The company had built a wardrobe-sized machine, the PI 180, which used a laser to write data on rhodium-coated plastic strips. It needed software, and nobody inside could write it. Outside firms were quoting huge sums.

__He spotted the opening and took it.__ He called Miner and Oates, and in summer 1977 the three bid $400,000. Their rivals were far higher, and Precision Instrument was at first suspicious that the price was too low. Miner and Oates each had a mortgage and young children. They reasoned that good programmers could always find another job, so the real risk was small.

items.label: what Ellison paid for 60% of the company
what Miner and Oates each paid, for 20%

blocks.text: They won it. In June 1977 they formed Software Development Laboratories, or SDL. They joked about names like Nero Systems before picking a plain one. Ellison took 60 percent because the push had been his, and Oates called it a bonus for chutzpah. Since Ellison stayed at Precision Instrument to supervise the contract, Miner became president. __Ellison was not even the first employee of his own company.__

Miner hired a fast young programmer, Bruce Scott, who began writing code with a pencil at home. In August they rented a ground-floor space with one window inside the Precision Instrument building in Santa Clara. When Scott asked how to get cables through a wall to the computer next door, Larry picked up a hammer and smashed a hole. Then he drove the whole company to San Jose to buy a sign. The whole company fitted in one used Mercedes.
He was 32, with $1,200 at stake. This is where it starts.

Look at how he got there. He had no degree, two dropped colleges, one failed marriage, and more than a decade of jobs he never truly loved. He told USC graduates that he only wanted a small place to work with talented friends and never expected more than 50 people. But one IBM research paper he had read in November 1976 was about to give that tiny firm a far bigger idea. That story comes next.

blocks.title: Your wasted years may not be wasted
blocks.text: From the outside, Larry's twenties looked like failure. Yet those years gave him deep knowledge of IBM machines, a salesman's nerve, and two partners far better at code than he was. Do not copy his debts or his exaggerations. Do copy this: keep learning, keep good people close, and move fast when a real opening appears.

factCheck.method: Built from Ellison's own interviews (Academy of Achievement 1997, Smithsonian oral history, USC 2016 speech), Vanity Fair 1997, The New York Times, Reuters and reference works, cross-checked against Mike Wilson's 1997 biography. Wilson's text was read from an unofficial online copy that is deliberately not cited; the book's catalogue record is cited instead, so every Wilson-only detail should be confirmed against a licensed copy. Most scenes rest on friends' memories gathered by Wilson and are attributed as such. Direct quotation is limited to one line; everything else is paraphrased in our own words. Exact ages for high-school pranks and lifeguard summers are not given in the sources, so none are stated.

disputed.note: Britannica-derived and Academy biographies say the Bronx. Ellison himself in the Academy interview, Wilson and The New York Times say the Lower East Side of Manhattan. The text says only New York City.
The New York Times says an Italian-American air force pilot; Wikipedia says Army Air Corps. The text says military pilot.

disputed.claim: Louis Ellison as a World War II bomber pilot
disputed.note: In the 1997 Academy interview Ellison said Louis was a bomber pilot in World War II. Louis arrived in the US in 1905 and no other source found supports this. Left out of the story as unverified.

disputed.claim: Louis Ellison's early wealth and politics
disputed.note: Sources agree he lost a real estate business in the Depression. Wilson could not confirm Ellison's claims that he was a millionaire, tennis champion or Congress candidate. Presented as Larry's claim.

Ellison has described the South Side as a bad neighbourhood and said he was raised there. Wilson says the family lived on the North Side until his high-school years, was not poor, and that South Shore was stable and middle class then. Both are shown.

disputed.claim: Why he left the University of Illinois
disputed.note: Vanity Fair, the Academy and Ellison credit his mother's death during finals, and report a science student of the year award. BusinessWeek (1995, as quoted by Wilson) reported that records showed dismissal for failing to maintain a C average after skipped finals. The university declined to tell Wilson. Both are shown. We could not find the award in university records.

disputed.claim: Timing of the first California trip and University of Chicago
disputed.note: Vanity Fair puts the first California summer in 1964 and enrolment that autumn; Wikipedia says summer 1966; Encyclopedia.com lists Chicago under 1966. Wilson reports one semester of registration and a permanent move in summer 1966. Text follows Vanity Fair and Wilson.

Vanity Fair says high-school maths and physics courses. Wilson and Ellison's Academy interview point to college, with Chicago's IBM 1401. Text follows the latter. Ellison also said he was a teenager when out-earning a professor, though he had turned 20 before reaching Chicago, so the text omits his age there.
This comes only from Ellison's own 2016 USC speech. No independent record was found, so it is attributed to him.

Encyclopedia.com and Wilson say divorce in 1974 after seven years, with Adda Quinn leaving, worn out by his spending and drift. Vanity Fair says they separated after barely two years and divorced five years later. Ellison's USC speech ties it to the sailboat. The text gives Wilson's and Ellison's versions.
Vanity Fair says he returned to Chicago and died in the 1980s. Wilson says he moved to an Oakland nursing home and died there. The text says only that they never made peace.

Ellison told the Smithsonian that Gene Amdahl invited him and called it one of his first jobs. Wilson says he joined in 1973 as a trainer and was laid off as non-essential. The Academy's phrase 'Amdahl colleagues' for Miner and Oates conflicts with nearly all accounts, which place their meeting at Ampex.
Britannica says he began at Ampex in 1973 and left in 1976. Wilson puts him at Amdahl in 1973 first. The timeline says about 1974 to 1976.

disputed.claim: Size of the Precision Instrument bid and rival bids
disputed.note: Ellison's 2007 keynote as reported by Philippine Star says $300,000, with the next bid at $2 million. Wilson and Bruce Scott say $400,000. Wilson also reports rival figures of $700,000 (Oates) and $2.3 million (Ellison). Text uses $400,000 and says rivals were far higher.
Wilson says Ellison $1,200 and Miner and Oates $400 each. Philippine Star says Ellison $1,200 and Miner $800. Forbes via Business Insider describes four founders pitching in. Text follows Wilson.

Oracle and Wikipedia give June 1977; Bruce Scott recalls August 1977; Wilson says formed in June with the first business day on 1 August. Wikipedia says Miner founded SDL and Ellison joined months later. Text follows Wilson.
Vanity Fair gives Universal Titanic Octopus, a daydream with Chuck Weiss. Wilson gives Intergalactic Tytanic Octopus as a joke name for SDL. Text uses the Vanity Fair version with Weiss.
Wilson describes a bought plastic sign; Ellison's 2007 keynote, as reported by Philippine Star, mentions a handwritten one. Text follows Wilson.
Vanity Fair and Business Insider say turquoise; Wilson says aqua blue. Trivial, and the text uses turquoise.
